en: Now, when it comes to tweaking those
settings, you can of course also remember
them so that they will be used in the future
again. So if you by default want, let's say,
10,000 tokens, you could save these settings
as a default so that you don't always have
to change it again when you reload the
model.
But you also have some advanced settings
here. Now, to be very honest, most of these
settings can stay the way they are. The
evaluation batch size is an interesting one
because here you can control the number of
input tokens that are processed at a time,
so simultaneously by the model.
And you could increase this to improve the
performance of the model at the cost of
using more memory.
But I typically keep the default here as
well. But you could experiment with
different values here.
The other settings, to be very honest, are
settings I never touch because the defaults
work quite well.
These ropey settings are about pushing the
boundaries of your model when it comes to
operating with lots of context. So long
context documents or chat histories. And I
typically prefer to split complex long
context tasks into simpler, shorter
subtasks, because in my experience, that
yields better results than operating on
super long context anyways.
Now, what is interesting are the flash
attention and the key and V-cache settings
down here though.
And the idea behind all these settings
especially when used together,
is that they can, as the tooltip tells us,
decrease the memory usage and also the
generation time of some models depending on
how well they support it.
Now, this quantization, this KV cache
quantization, is not the quantization we
were referring to earlier in the course when
we explored hardware requirements.
Instead, flash attention and KV cache
quantization, these 3 settings in the end
work together
As you also see here, flash attention must
be enabled for V-cache quantization at
least. And the idea behind these settings is
that the model has to process less tokens to
generate a new output token, because
normally
it always has to process all existing
tokens, including existing output tokens it
generated, to produce the next token in
line, which makes sense because that next
token depends on all these other tokens. Now
with flash attention and KV cache
quantization enabled,
roughly speaking, tokens generated in
earlier steps can be cached and therefore be
remembered and can therefore be reused in
subsequent steps to generate future tokens
without having to recalculate them because
without this turned on, the model
essentially recalculates all previous tokens
just to derive that next token.
With flash attention and disk caching
enabled, it can simply load
those old calculations from memory and
therefore derive the next token quicker.
Now, at the point of time where I'm
recording this, this is an experimental
feature. And as this message here tells us,
it may cause issues with
because not all models are
great at using this mechanism or are aware
of this technique.

this on and simply experiment with the model
with that being turned on to see whether it
makes a difference and whether it works well
for you.
For example, here with that turned on,
if I now ask it to
write an essay
about a rabbit,
it's quite quick at doing so.

it of course again goes ahead and generates
a text.
And for me here, it generated 1,000 tokens
at a rate of only 23 tokens per second. So
quite a bit slower than with flash attention
turned on.
And that's precisely the idea behind flash
attention and KV caching.
The idea is to give you faster generations,
but you should carefully check whether the
results are good or if your model is having
any problems with these settings. In that
case, you should of course turn off these
settings.
But from all these more advanced settings,
these are the ones I would consider turning
on to get faster inference.
